n: Paul opens his letter with Timothy at his side, writing to the whole branch of Saints in Philippi and their local leaders. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia and the first place in Europe where Paul planted the gospel.

f.g: Local Church officers: “bishops” (Greek episkopoi, overseers) presided; deacons (diakonoi) served under them.

n: Paul’s usual greeting blends the Greek “grace” (God’s unearned help and favor) with the Hebrew “peace” (shalom, wholeness). Both come from the Father and the Son together.

f.g: Greek charis — gift, favor, divine enabling help.

n: Every time Paul thinks of the Philippians, it turns into gratitude. This is one of his warmest letters; the Philippians had supported him faithfully for years.
His prayers for them are not anxious or heavy but full of joy. “Joy” and “rejoice” run through this letter more than any other Paul wrote, even though he writes from prison.
“Fellowship” means partnership. From the day Lydia was baptized, the Philippians had shared in Paul’s work with their faith, prayers, and money.

f.g: Greek koinōnia — sharing, partnership, common participation.

n: Paul is sure that God, who started a good work in them, will keep working until it is finished at Christ’s Second Coming. God does not abandon a work He begins in a willing heart.

f.g: The Second Coming, when Christ returns in glory to judge and reign.
Finish, bring to completion.

n: It is fitting (“meet”) for Paul to feel this way because he holds them in his heart. Whether he is in chains or defending the gospel in court, they share with him in the same grace.

f.g: Fitting, right, proper.
Chains; Paul’s imprisonment.

n: Paul calls God as his witness that he longs for them with the very tenderness of Christ. In KJV English the “bowels” were considered the seat of deep feeling, as we would say “the heart.”

f.g: Inward affections, deep compassion — the heart.
God is my witness.

n: His prayer is that their love will keep growing, guided by real knowledge and wise discernment. Love without understanding can be misdirected; Paul wants both together.

f.g: Discernment, moral perception.

n: With discerning love they can recognize and choose what is truly best, and live with pure motives, not causing others to stumble, until Christ comes.

f.g: Greek eilikrinēs — pure, unmixed; tested in sunlight and found genuine.
Not stumbling and not causing others to stumble.

n: The good fruit in their lives comes through Jesus Christ, and all of it brings glory to God. Righteousness here is not self-made but grows from being connected to Christ.
Paul wants them to know that his imprisonment has not stopped the gospel; it has actually helped it spread. Hardship became an opportunity.

f.g: Progress, advancement.

n: Everyone in the “palace” — likely the Praetorian Guard, the emperor’s elite soldiers who took turns guarding Paul — now knows he is a prisoner because of Christ, not for a crime.

f.g: Greek praitōrion — the Praetorian Guard or the governor’s headquarters.

n: Seeing Paul’s courage in chains, many other believers have grown bolder in sharing the gospel. His example strengthened them instead of scaring them.

f.g: Growing confident.

n: Not everyone preaching Christ has good motives. Some are driven by jealousy and rivalry toward Paul; others preach out of genuine goodwill.

f.g: Jealousy and rivalry.

n: The rivals preach to compete with Paul, hoping to make his imprisonment more painful by outshining or embarrassing him.

f.g: Selfish ambition, factional rivalry.

n: The others preach out of love, understanding that Paul has been appointed to defend the gospel and supporting that mission.

f.g: Appointed, placed for a purpose.

n: Paul’s remarkable response: what matters most is that Christ is being preached, whatever the motive. He refuses to let personal rivalry steal his joy.

f.g: False motives, outward show.

n: Paul trusts that their prayers and the help of the Spirit of Christ will bring about his deliverance — whether release from prison or ultimate salvation.

f.g: Greek sōtēria — rescue, deliverance; possibly here release from prison.
Full provision, generous support.

n: His deepest hope is never to shrink back in shame, but to honor Christ by how he lives — or by how he dies, if it comes to that.

f.g: Made great, honored, shown to be glorious.

n: One of Paul’s most famous lines: his whole life is about Christ, and death would only bring him closer to Christ. Either way, he cannot lose.
If he keeps living, that means more fruitful work for the Lord. So he honestly does not know which he would choose.

f.g: Know.

n: Paul feels pulled in two directions. Part of him longs to leave mortality and be with Christ, which would be far better for him personally.

f.g: A tight place; hard-pressed between two choices.
Between.
Greek analuō — to loosen, as in breaking camp or untying a ship to set sail.

n: But staying alive is more needed for the Saints’ sake. Paul puts their spiritual needs ahead of his own desire for rest.
Paul feels confident that he will remain alive and continue serving them so their faith can grow and bring them joy.

f.g: Progress, growth.

n: When he comes back to visit them, their rejoicing in Christ will overflow. Many believe Paul was indeed released from this first Roman imprisonment.
Whatever happens to Paul, they should live in a way worthy of the gospel, standing together in unity of spirit and purpose, like a team striving side by side.

f.g: Way of life, conduct. Greek politeuesthe — live as citizens, a fitting word for a Roman colony.
Contending side by side, like athletes or soldiers.

n: Do not be frightened by opponents. Their hostility is a sign that they are on the path to ruin, while your courage is evidence that God is saving you.

f.g: Startled, spooked — like a frightened horse.
Destruction, ruin.

n: Paul presents suffering for Christ as a privilege “given” to them, a gift alongside the gift of faith. Disciples share in their Lord’s experiences.
The Philippians had seen Paul beaten and jailed in their own city, and now hear of his Roman chains. They face the same kind of struggle he does.

f.g: Greek agōn — struggle, contest, as in an athletic arena.
